profile.text: The narrator: an army doctor sent home from Afghanistan after a wound at Maiwand and a bad fever, now alone in London with a small pension and little money.

facets.text: The narrator. Qualified as a doctor in London in 1878 and joined the army as an assistant surgeon, reaching his regiment in the Second Afghan War.
Hit in the shoulder by a Jezail bullet at the battle of Maiwand; his orderly Murray got him back to British lines.
Nearly died of enteric fever while recovering in Peshawar and was shipped home to England with his health ruined.
Alone in London with no family and a small army pension, he is running short of money and looking for cheaper lodgings.
Owns up to keeping a bull pup, having frayed nerves, rising at odd hours and being very lazy.
With poor health, no visitors and little to do, he becomes absorbed in trying to work out who Holmes really is.
Suspects that Holmes's confident deductions are bluster that cannot be checked.
His health has still not recovered from the Afghan campaign.
Has written up the Jefferson Hope case as a short book titled "A Study in Scarlet".
Has now lived with Holmes in Baker Street for years.
Watson's orderly at Maiwand, who saved him by throwing him across a pack-horse and carrying him to safety.
Battle of the Second Afghan War where Watson was badly wounded.
Once a dresser under Watson at Barts; the two run into each other by chance at the Criterion Bar.
Takes Watson to the hospital laboratory and introduces him to Sherlock Holmes.
The London hospital where Watson and Stamford once worked together.
Holmes works in its chemical laboratory, a high room crowded with bottles, retorts and test-tubes.
The London bar where Watson meets Stamford again.

profile.text: Watson's companion of several years in Baker Street, who calls himself the only unofficial consulting detective and turns to cocaine when he has no problem to work on.

facets.text: A man Stamford knows from the hospital's chemical laboratory, who is looking for someone to split the cost of a set of rooms.
Knows anatomy well and is a first-rate chemist, yet has never studied medicine systematically; even Stamford does not know his aims.
Stamford finds him scientific to the point of coldness: he has been seen beating corpses in the dissecting rooms to study bruising after death.
On first meeting Watson, tells him he has been in Afghanistan, and will not say how he knew.
Has just discovered a reagent that reacts to haemoglobin, giving a reliable test for bloodstains, and is thrilled by its value in criminal cases.
Warns Watson that he smokes strong tobacco, keeps chemicals and runs experiments at home, and sometimes falls silent for days.
Over six feet tall and very lean, with piercing eyes, a hawk-like nose, a square chin, and hands stained by ink and chemicals.
Knows next to nothing of literature, philosophy or politics, and did not know that the earth goes round the sun.
Treats the mind as an attic with limited room, so he deliberately forgets anything that is no use to his work.

Watson's list of his knowledge: none in literature, philosophy or astronomy; profound in chemistry; immense in sensational crime; also a fine violinist, boxer, swordsman and singlestick player who knows British law.
Receives a stream of very different visitors he calls clients, borrowing the shared sitting-room to see them.
Turns out to be the author of the magazine article on observation that Watson has just mocked.
Works as a consulting detective, perhaps the only one in the world: police and private detectives bring him cases they cannot solve.
Explains that he read Watson's army bearing, tanned face, fair wrists, haggard look and stiff arm in an instant to place him in Afghanistan.
Scorns the famous fictional detectives Dupin and Lecoq.
Identifies a messenger across the street as a retired Marine sergeant; the man confirms it.
Has been injecting cocaine several times a day for months when he has no case, which alarms Watson.
Calls himself the only unofficial consulting detective, the last resort of official detectives such as Gregson, Lestrade and Athelney Jones; he wants no public credit.
Thinks Watson's written account of their first case was spoiled by romance, since detection should be treated as an exact science.

history.text: A young man who works in the hospital's chemical laboratory: a first-class chemist who knows anatomy well but follows no regular course of study, and who wants someone to share rooms with.
His profession is a mystery to Watson: he is not studying medicine or working toward any degree, yet his knowledge in certain areas is deep and exact.

Watson's fellow lodger in Baker Street: a tall, very lean man with sharp eyes and a beak of a nose, who earns his living as a consulting detective, reasoning from small observed details to firm conclusions.

facets.text: A chemical test Holmes has just devised that reacts only to haemoglobin, detecting even tiny traces of blood.
Holmes has his eye on a suite of rooms here that would suit two lodgers.
Two bedrooms and a bright, well-furnished sitting-room. Holmes and Watson take the rooms on the spot and move in.
A small, sallow, dark-eyed visitor who calls on Holmes three or four times in one week.
A well-known detective; Holmes says he came for help after getting lost in a forgery case.
Named by Holmes as one of the official detectives who come to him when out of their depth.
A magazine article Watson reads over breakfast, claiming a trained observer can read a person's thoughts and history from tiny details.
Watson dismisses it as nonsense.
Holmes reveals that he wrote it.
Holmes's name for his own trade: detectives and private clients bring him their problems and he usually solves them from what they tell him, often without leaving his room.
Poe's fictional detective. Watson compares Holmes to him; Holmes thinks Dupin showy, superficial and overrated.
Gaboriau's fictional detective, whom Holmes dismisses as a bungler with nothing going for him but energy.
A man walking down Baker Street whom Holmes, at a glance, calls a retired sergeant of Marines.
Delivers a letter to Holmes. Now a commissionaire, he confirms he served as a sergeant in the Royal Marine Light Infantry.
An official detective Holmes names among those who bring him cases.
An official detective Holmes names among those who bring him cases.

events.summary: Watson is wounded at the battle of Maiwand.
Watson runs into Stamford at the Criterion Bar.
Stamford introduces Watson to Holmes at Barts.
Holmes and Watson agree to share rooms.
Holmes reveals he wrote "The Book of Life".
Holmes explains that he is a consulting detective.
A messenger confirms Holmes's guess that he was a Marine sergeant.
Watson confronts Holmes about his cocaine habit.

recap.text: Watson and Holmes settle into 221B Baker Street. Puzzled by Holmes's lopsided knowledge and many visitors, Watson finally learns that Holmes wrote an article on deduction and works as a consulting detective. Holmes then proves his point by identifying a messenger as a former Marine sergeant.
